o: For each index i we must count occurrences of nums[i] strictly beyond position i+k. Equivalently, ans[i] equals the frequency of nums[i] in the suffix starting at i+k+1. In [1,2,1,1] with k=1: for i=0 the eligible suffix is indices 2..3 containing two 1s → 2; for i=1 the suffix is index 3 (value 1 ≠ 2) → 0; later indices have empty suffixes → 0. With n up to 1e5, recomputing each suffix naively is O(n²); instead sweep right-to-left while maintaining a running frequency map of the current eligible suffix, adding index i+k+1 exactly when i decreases past it.
k: ans[i] is a suffix frequency query: count of nums[i] in positions > i+k.
A right-to-left sweep lets one hash map serve all queries incrementally.
Index i+k+1 enters the window precisely when the pointer moves from i+1 to i.

a.n: Approach 1: Reverse Sweep with Frequency Map
a.i: Iterate i from n-1 down to 0. Before answering index i, insert nums[i+k+1] into the counter (if in range) — at that moment the counter holds frequencies of exactly the indices in (i+k, n-1]. Then ans[i] = counter[nums[i]]. Each element is inserted once and read once.
s: Create ans of size n and an empty hash map cnt.
For i from n-1 downto 0: if i+k+1 < n, increment cnt[nums[i+k+1]].
a.t: O(n) — each index is inserted into and queried from the map exactly once.
a.sp: O(n) — the hash map holds at most n distinct entries.

a.i: Group all positions of each value into sorted lists during one forward pass. For query i, the answer is the number of stored positions of nums[i] greater than i+k, found via bisect/upper_bound on that value's list. This shines if queries arrive online or you need per-value statistics.
s: Build pos[v] = sorted list of indices where nums equals v.
For each i, binary-search pos[nums[i]] for the first index > i+k.
ans[i] = list length minus that position.
a.t: O(n log n) — building the lists is linear; each of the n queries binary-searches its value's list.
a.sp: O(n) — all positions stored across lists.

w: Approach 1 is the interview favorite: linear time, tiny code, obviously correct window semantics. Pitfalls: off-by-one on the boundary (window is strictly j > i+k, hence inserting i+k+1), handling k = n-1 (every window is empty), and confusing this with a sliding-window distinct-count problem. Follow-ups: answer queries for varying k (position lists handle that gracefully), or stream the input left-to-right (would require a different structure like a BIT over values).
